explanation: Fires on middle subword pieces of long, often technical or foreign words (e.g. 'cant[on]', 'stal[ag]mites', 'p[oly]acrylamide', 'cep[hal]ic', 'pyram[idal]'), plus some unrelated tokens ('ellipse', 'Accept'). No shared meaning; the only loose pattern is a word fragment inside a multi-token word.

Fires most strongly on the class-name part of a constructor declaration, where a class name is repeated as a method name (e.g. 'public Generic[Repository]()', 'Vertice3f::Vertice3[f](', 'FastJSON[Result](object'). It also fires on the space after 'Solve' in math word problems and on assorted tokens in prose and science text.

Fires on the first digit of the day number in a date ('May [1]9', 'July [2]2', 'On [1]2 September', '2006-08-[0]2'), and often on the first digit of a year. It also fires on early function-word tokens near the start of a text ('What does [it]', 'Here's [a]', 'and [of] all').

Fires on tokens in generated algebra problems: the space or 'Solve' after 'Solve', minus signs, and digits inside numbers ('Solve[ ]0*g', ', [-]2*l', '91[0]*m'). It also fires on license and boilerplate punctuation ('this library[;] see the file COPYING', 'www.oracle[.com]'). Weak on ordinary prose.

Fires on structural tokens in code, config and paths: key names in config or connection strings ('Port', 'port', quoted keys), path separators and segments ('/version', '\', '/meta'), ':' before a port number, digits in patent URLs. It also fires on scattered prose tokens (', ', 'women', 'car'), so beyond code syntax the pattern is mixed.

Fires on the first subword piece of a word split into several tokens, mostly in French, Portuguese or scientific text ('[ré]duit', '[desenv]olvendo', '[pl]unger', 'sulfadoxine[-p]yrimethamine', '[unre]strained'), and on accented-character byte pieces. Fires mostly when the token starts a word that continues in the next token.

Fires on mixed tokens: medical word pieces ('myocard'-ial, 'di[aphrag]m', 'sac[ro]iliitis'), the word 'of' in sentence-initial 'One of', code string literals and template arguments ('"[class]"', '"[dd]/MM'), and Japanese verb endings. No single concept.

Fires on several unrelated things: legal-case wording ('appeals' after a party name, 'for' in 'for appellant/appellee'), auto-generated-code notices ('DO NOT [EDIT]', 'do not [modify]'), the comma after a dateline or appositive, and assorted prose tokens. A mixture.

Fires on internal subword pieces of chemical and biochemical compound names, especially phosphate-related ones ('triph[osph]atase', 'phosph[at]ase', 'farn[es]yl', 'meth[ion]ine', 'thiog[uan]ine'). Weaker on other long technical words. Context must be chemistry or biomedicine.

Fires on tokens inside code expressions, especially function-call and argument syntax ('[paste]0(', 'make_pair[(x]', '%[2]', '[k]', '" [+] name', '[$]8'). In prose it fires on 'per' in rate phrases ('$100,000 [per] session', '1.5 [per] 100'). Mostly code-syntax tokens, plus the separate 'per' rate pattern.

Fires on a wide mixture: 'CIR'/'CU' pieces in 'CIRCUIT' in court headers, 'of' in 'out of', code punctuation and quotes after whitespace padding, spaces before numbers, and prepositions such as 'by' and 'para'. No coherent concept.

Fires on Chinese and Japanese characters (e.g. '語', '版', '質'), on mid-word code identifier pieces ('param[etrize]', 'Qsci[Lexer]', 'MOCK[_METHOD]'), and on assorted English phrase tokens ('passed [away]', 'in [accordance]', 'broad [sense]'). A mixture.

Fires on the second token of a word, right after a capital or lowercase 'h'/'th' piece ('TH[OM]PKINS', 'H[ann]arah', 'h[ollow]', 'h[olly]', 'th[imer]osal', 'H[OM]WARP'). It responds to a word-continuation piece after an 'h'-initial fragment, mostly in names and rare words.

Fires most strongly on Devanagari (Hindi) vowel-sign or byte pieces. Moderately on pieces of Italian words and of Italian or Indian personal names ('Gi[ud]ice', 'R[ond]inella', 'Gaurav[ Rath]ore', '[ Paolo]'). Roughly: script and name pieces from Indian or Italian text.
